web_title: 3. Cash Conversion, Working Capital & the Raw-Material Chain
question: When the profit is reported, how much of it arrives as cash, and what has to stay true in the supply chain for that to continue?

epigraph.quote: We do not have long term supply contracts with our raw material suppliers, and therefore, we are subject to the risk of increases in the costs of raw materials.
epigraph.author: Stallion Red Herring Prospectus, risk factors, 11 January 2025 [6]

web_blocks.html: Profit is an opinion until the cash arrives. For a refrigerant business the cash story runs through three places: the raw material bought from abroad, the inventory held to meet orders, and the credit given to customers. This chapter follows each one through the FY26 audited figures and the RHP’s disclosures, and it tests two bear points against the filings.

web_blocks.title: Where the raw material comes from

web_blocks.html: The raw-material side is the largest and least secure part of the chain. The RHP says import costs were 85.00% of revenue from operations in the six months to September 2024, up from 70.23% in FY23 [6]. China supplied 92.97% of those imports in the same period [6]. The RHP is direct about what follows: “We do not have long term supply contracts with our raw material suppliers, and therefore, we are subject to the risk of increases in the costs of raw materials.” [6]

On the August 2026 call, an analyst asked about sourcing, and management’s answer shows why the contract gap matters. Management said: “Now to have anything to have value has to be iron-clad. And iron-clad will mean time-bound supply after which the penalties start enhancing. So it’s not in the best interest of the company.” [9] It also expected a glut of AHF supply by 2028, which it called a buyer’s market [9]. Both are management’s views. The sources contain no supply contract behind either one.

web_blocks.title: The FY26 cost waterfall, per ₹100 of revenue

web_blocks.html: The waterfall takes FY26 audited revenue from operations of ₹430.68 crore and scales every line to ₹100 of revenue. It reconciles to audited profit after tax of ₹43.84 crore, so each line is an audited figure and no line is estimated.

web_blocks.caption: Audited FY26 cost waterfall, scaled to ₹100 of revenue from operations

lines.label: Change in inventories
lines.note: Audited change in inventories of −₹2,395.94 lakh, booked as a credit to cost because inventory rose [1]

web_blocks.takeaway: Materials take ₹85.70 of every ₹100 of revenue. The inventory credit adds back ₹5.56, and tax takes ₹3.52. What is left is ₹10.18 of profit after tax. The statements give no product-level split, so this margin is for the company as a whole.

web_blocks.html: The inventory credit is the line to watch. The ₹23.96 crore credit to cost came from holding more finished inventory at the end of the year than at the start [1]. The cost sits on the balance sheet until that inventory is sold, so the margin benefits in the year the inventory is built and the cost lands later. On the August call, an analyst asked how much of the quarter’s EBITDA came from inventory gains. Management replied: “It’s a mix, 50:50.” [9] That is an answer about one quarter, not the full year, and no filing gives the split.

Put a number on the raw-material exposure. The FY26 waterfall has materials at about ₹85.70 of every ₹100 of revenue, and profit after tax at about ₹10.18 [1]. So a rise of 1% in material cost alone, before any pass-through to customers, takes about ₹0.86 of profit out of every ₹100 of revenue. That is roughly 8% of the year’s profit from a single percentage point. With no long-term contract, the company carries that sensitivity itself.

web_blocks.title: Working capital: customers paid faster, inventory stayed heavy

web_blocks.html: Trade receivables fell from ₹105.54 crore at March 2025 to ₹77.53 crore at March 2026 [1]. Inventory at March 2026 was ₹126.63 crore, and the audited change in inventories shows it rose by about ₹24 crore over the year [1]. The ratio series shows the effect in days. Debtor days fell from 102 to 66, while inventory days edged up from 128 to 134 [24]. Days payable fell from 27 to 19, so the company now pays its suppliers faster than it did a year earlier [24].

Put the days into money, roughly. FY26 revenue of ₹430.68 crore works out to about ₹1.18 crore of sales a day. The 36-day fall in debtor days is therefore worth roughly ₹42 crore of cash, released once. That is a real gain, but it does not repeat every year, so the next gain has to come from sales or margin [1][24].

web_blocks.caption: Working capital days, years to 31 March (Screener ratio series)
rows: Inventory held slightly longer again in FY26
Cycle shortened by 23 days in FY26
web_blocks.takeaway: The 23-day shortening came mostly from customers paying faster, a 36-day gain. Suppliers being paid sooner and inventory held longer took back about 14 days of that. The cycle is shorter, but the inventory line is not improving.

web_blocks.title: A BEAR POINT THE FILINGS DO NOT SUPPORT
paragraphs: A common bear point says receivables jumped in FY26. The audited balance sheet shows the opposite. Trade receivables fell from ₹105.54 crore to ₹77.53 crore [1]. What did rise sharply is cash and bank balances. Cash and cash equivalents were ₹212.47 crore and bank balances were ₹221.20 crore at March 2026, both after the rights issue [1][23].
Keep the two claims apart. A rise in receivables would mean customers were taking longer to pay. The filings show the reverse, so the bear point should be rewritten rather than repeated.

web_blocks.title: Cash conversion: H1 FY27 reverses back to negative

web_blocks.html: Operating cash flow was ₹39.36 crore in FY26, against profit after tax of ₹43.84 crore—a conversion of about 0.90 times, after negative operating cash flow of −₹73 crore in FY24 and −₹13.43 crore in FY25 [14][1][4]. The H1 FY27 filing (six months ended 30 September 2026) shows FY26 was not yet a durable habit: operating cash flow swung back to negative −₹39.17 crore (−₹3,916.92 lakh) despite ₹30.53 crore of profit before tax [14][36]. Even as inventories fell from ₹126.63 crore to ₹97.12 crore and trade receivables dropped from ₹77.53 crore to ₹67.27 crore, Other Current Assets surged more than sevenfold from ₹22.42 crore to ₹160.88 crore—primarily ₹129 crore of capital advances for Bhilwara’s EPC contract plus supplier advances [14][36][38].

Asked about the return to negative operating cash flow on the 19 November 2026 earnings call, the Chairman & CEO dismissed cash-flow scrutiny outright, stating that “cash flow is not a true reflection of anything” and questioning “how anyone is checking the health of a company by the cash flow” [36]. For an import-heavy blender whose cumulative six-year operating cash flow (FY21–FY26) was already deeply negative before H1 FY27’s −₹39.17 crore outflow [14][36], dismissing cash conversion is a serious financial-discipline warning.

web_blocks.title: Raw-material shocks, anti-dumping friction & FX pass-through limits

web_blocks.html: Q2 FY27 demonstrated the arithmetic of material sensitivity in real time. Raw-material expenses jumped 38.95% year on year to ₹116.79 crore (85.9% of sales) against 28.86% revenue growth [14][36]. Management attributed the squeeze to 10% to 20% Gulf material-price spikes, over 20% freight escalation, and aggressive quota-year import selling [36]. Two structural frictions compound that exposure: first, customers rarely honor contractual foreign-exchange pass-through clauses in practice, as management acknowledged in earlier calls [9]; second, on 18 September 2026, India’s Directorate General of Trade Remedies (DGTR) recommended extending anti-dumping duties on Chinese HFC R-32 imports for another five years (Case No. AD (SSR)-11/2025) [41], adding persistent landed-cost friction to Stallion’s import-and-blend model until Bhilwara reaches stable production.

The FY26 investing outflow of ₹253 crore was mostly ₹205.13 crore placed in fixed deposits alongside ₹49.31 crore of actual plant spending [14][23]. In H1 FY27, deployment accelerated sharply: Fixed Assets plus Capital Work-in-Progress more than doubled from ₹65.60 crore (March 2026) to ₹145.97 crore (September 2026), while cash and bank balances fell ₹141.97 crore from ₹433.67 crore to ₹291.70 crore [14][36]. Two SEBI-mandated Monitoring Agency reports filed on 14 November 2026 expose critical capital-allocation and internal-control details omitted from headline summaries [37][38]:

First, Infomerics Valuation & Rating Limited reported that ₹278.29 crore of the ₹363.93 crore Rights Issue had been utilized by 30 September 2026—including ₹232.08 crore for plant construction, ₹10.21 crore for land, and ₹36.00 crore (9.9% of gross proceeds) consumed by rights-issue expenses [38]. Notably, EPC contractor Pansen Engineering India Pvt Ltd (estimated civil contract ₹269.76 crore) operates on a cost-plus 10% basis; Stallion paid ₹78.00 crore in Q2 FY27 as on-account advances before invoices are raised upon structure completion, so Infomerics explicitly stated it was unable to map individual payments to invoices and had reviewed only a partial contract copy [38]. By the 19 November call, management said only about ₹50 crore of rights proceeds remained, while Bhilwara incurred a ~₹40 crore cost overrun (90+ ISO-tank containers and equipment) and Mambattu faced a ₹10–15 crore shortfall [36][37].

Second, CARE Ratings’ Q2 FY27 IPO Monitoring Agency report qualified IPO fund utilization as “Deviation from the objects: Yes” (₹0.40 crore paid from company cash instead of liquidating an IPO fixed deposit), flagged commingling of funds across routine operating accounts (₹2.49 crore claimed as reimbursements), documented prior excess issue expenses of ₹3.99 crore misclassified under working capital in management and CA certificates (retroactively regularized via a 3 June 2026 special resolution), and warned that higher spending on working capital and Khalapur reduced funds left for Mambattu, potentially impacting object viability [37]. Looking ahead, combined gross cash uses across R-32 start-up working capital (₹150 crore), the Bhilwara cost overrun (₹40 crore), the Mambattu shortfall (₹10–15 crore), and the proposed Hurda HFO plant (₹200 crore) sum to ₹400–₹405 crore (₹350 crore for R-32 working capital and HFO capex alone) [36][37]. Management’s signaled ~₹200 crore represents the incremental external raise expected on top of roughly ₹50 crore of remaining rights-issue cash, internal operating accruals, the unused ₹120 crore bank overdraft facility, and phased late-2027 HFO capex timing (deferred until three to five months after Bhilwara R-32 stabilizes) [36].

web_blocks.title: NARRATOR’S REFLECTION
paragraphs: Pause on the cash cycle and the monitoring reports together. FY26’s debtor-day improvement released cash once, and H1 FY27 immediately swung back to −₹39.17 crore of operating cash flow as ₹129 crore moved into unmapped cost-plus EPC advances [36][38]. When a management team dismisses operating cash flow as irrelevant while signaling a third capital raise in two years, cash-flow forensics move to the center of the analysis [36].

Hold the import and tariff facts next to it. With 85% import cost intensity, no long-term raw-material contracts, unhonored FX pass-through, and DGTR recommending five more years of anti-dumping duty on Chinese R-32, spreads remain exposed every quarter that Bhilwara stays uncommissioned [6][41].

book_paragraphs: Let me start with a simple question. When the company reports a profit, how much of it do you actually receive in cash? For a refrigerant business that question is not academic. The business buys its main raw material from abroad, holds inventory so it can meet orders, and gives customers time to pay. Each of those three steps ties up money, and each can turn a profit on paper into a shortage in the bank.

The raw material is the first thing to understand. The RHP says import costs were 85% of revenue in the six months to September 2024, up from about 70% in FY23. China supplied almost all of the imports in that period, at 92.97%. And the company says plainly that it has no long-term supply contracts with those suppliers. In Q2 FY27 that vulnerability showed up directly: raw-material expense jumped nearly 39% year on year to 116.79 crore on Gulf supply inflation, higher freight, and quota-year selling pressure. Customers rarely honor FX escalation clauses in practice, and in September 2026 India’s DGTR recommended extending anti-dumping duties on Chinese R-32 for another five years—adding further landed-cost friction until Stallion manufactures its own molecule.

Now look at the FY26 waterfall. Take every rupee of revenue and see where it goes. Of each hundred rupees of revenue, about eighty-six went on materials. The inventory build gave back about five and a half, because the company held more finished product at year end. Employees, other costs, interest and depreciation took a few more. Tax took about three and a half. What was left was about ten rupees of profit after tax. That is a thin margin on a large base of purchased material, and it is why a small move in input cost matters so much.

The inventory credit deserves a careful look. When inventory rises, the cost of the goods you have not yet sold sits on the balance sheet, and that lifts the reported margin in the year it happens. It does not stay there forever. Management was asked on the August call how much of the quarter’s earnings came from inventory gains, and it said the split was about fifty-fifty. That is an answer about one quarter. It tells you the company itself sees a real share of its earnings coming from timing, and that the full-year split is not in any filing.

The working capital story has a good half and a tougher half. Customers paid faster in FY26, cutting debtor days from 102 to 66, and trade receivables declined further to 67.27 crore by September 2026 while inventories eased to 97.12 crore. Yet Other Current Assets exploded from 22.42 crore to 160.88 crore in six months, driven by 129 crore of capital advances to Bhilwara’s EPC contractor and supplier advances. That pushed H1 FY27 operating cash flow back to negative 39.17 crore despite 30.53 crore of pre-tax profit.

There is a bear point circulating that says receivables jumped in FY26. The audited balance sheet says the opposite: receivables fell both in FY26 and in H1 FY27. The real cash drain was not unpaid customer bills—it was working-capital and capital-advance outflows that turned operating cash flow negative again in H1 FY27. Even more concerning, when asked about negative cash flow on the 19 November 2026 call, the CEO stated that cash flow is not a true reflection of anything. Investors should treat that attitude toward cash conversion as a governance warning.

Now separate spending from monitoring-agency controls. In FY26 most of the 253 crore investing outflow went into fixed deposits (205 crore), with only 49 crore on plants. In H1 FY27, Fixed Assets plus CWIP jumped from 65.60 crore to 145.97 crore, and cash fell from 433.67 crore to 291.70 crore. The 14 November 2026 monitoring reports reveal friction under the hood: Infomerics showed 278.29 crore of the 363.93 crore rights issue already utilized (including 36 crore—nearly 10% of gross proceeds—on issue expenses) and noted that advances to civil EPC contractor Pansen Engineering are paid on a cost-plus 10% basis before invoicing, preventing invoice-level mapping. Separately, CARE Ratings qualified the IPO monitoring report for a 0.40 crore deviation, flagged commingling of funds in routine operating accounts, and noted that overspending on working capital and Khalapur left less IPO funding for Mambattu.

Combined gross outlays across the 40 crore Bhilwara cost overrun, Mambattu’s 10 to 15 crore shortfall, 150 crore of anticipated R-32 start-up working capital, and 200 crore of planned HFO capex total 400 to 405 crore. Because Stallion has nearly exhausted both its IPO and rights-issue proceeds, management’s signaled 200 crore represents the incremental external fundraise expected alongside roughly 50 crore of remaining rights cash, internal operating accruals, the unused 120 crore bank overdraft facility, and phased late-2027 HFO spending. Falling debtor days release cash only once; sustained capital intensity without positive operating cash flow forces repeated external financing.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR’S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Imagine you are the person who has to pay the raw material bill next quarter, with no contract to protect you. Then ask whether the cash you have on hand covers that bill for as long as it takes to collect from customers. The answer tells you more about this business than the margin in any single quarter.
